cards.text: Friend, the Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), has spent a while watching people chase the wind (Ecclesiastes 4:16). Now he walks us up to the house of God. And the first thing he tells us at the door is to guard our steps.

cards.question: At the house of God, the Teacher says to draw near to ___ rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools.
The Teacher says the fools who offer the sacrifice of fools at the house of God know they are doing wrong.

cards.text: Next he goes after the mouth: don't be quick to speak, and don't be hasty in your heart to utter a word before God. Friend, that's me answering the group chat before I finish READING it, FIVE replies deep in the WRONG conversation.

cards.question: The Teacher says to let your words be few before God. What reason does he give?

answers.text: God is in heaven and you are on earth
God already knows what you will say
God listens best to quiet hearts

cards.text: Then he paints a picture: as a dream comes through many cares. You know the one, friend, that stressed-out week when you dream your boss is a goose running the Monday meeting.

cards.question: In the Teacher's picture, a dream comes through many cares. Whose speech does he say comes with many words?

cards.text: Now the Teacher turns to vows made to God. I promised my oven a clean rack back in March, friend, and that oven has NOT forgotten.

cards.question: The Teacher says that once you make a vow to God, you can take your time fulfilling it.
Don't delay in fulfilling a vow, the Teacher says, because God takes no pleasure in ___.
The Teacher weighs two choices about vows to God. Which does he say is better?

answers.text: Not making a vow at all
Making a vow and not fulfilling it
Making a vow only in private

cards.text: Then comes the warning: don't let your mouth cause your flesh to sin. Your mouth signs up for the job, friend, and the REST of you has to show up Monday morning and do it.

cards.question: The Teacher says not to tell the messenger that your vow was a ___.
If your words make God angry, what does the Teacher say could happen to the work of your hands?

answers.text: Others could take credit for it

cards.text: He brings the dream picture back one last time: as many dreams bring futility, so do many words. Like that goose-boss dream, friend, a big pile of words goes NOWHERE.

cards.question: After all those warnings about words and vows, what does the Teacher tell us to do?

findings.problem: Card 1 only says the Teacher walks us to the house of God and tells us to guard our steps. Nothing before this card points toward listening, so picking 'listen' over 'sing' or 'give' comes down to luck or to guessing the next word of the line. The story card needs more context, or the card should ask a different question.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: The verse's core action is the mouth causing the flesh to sin. The joke's action is the mouth committing you to a job that the rest of you then shows up and does. That matches keeping a commitment, not sinning, so the comparison doesn't share the verse's action.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The question says the Teacher 'weighs two choices,' but 'Making a vow only in private' isn't one of the two choices being weighed. The question's own framing rules that answer out. After cards 9 and 10, 'Making a vow and not fulfilling it' is also clearly not the better one, so the right answer is left standing alone.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.
